Quantifying a known compound requires three steps: finding its peak in every run,
integrating it, and converting the area to a concentration using a calibration 
curve. Targeted analysis integrates only the peaks at known retention times:
`get_peaks(targets = ...)` fits the peaks near the retention times you list,
and `get_peaktable()` returns one named column per target.

This article quantifies four compounds in a dilution series whose retention
times drift. It aligns the runs to find the targets, integrates the unaligned
runs, fits calibration curves, and compares the areas with those from the
instrument's own software.

```{r setup}
library(chromatographR)
```

## Reading the standards

The example is a dilution series of a mixed standard of four benzoxazinoids
(DIBOA, DIMBOA, BOA and MBOA), from 1000 to 4 ppm, plus a methanol blank. It
ships with chromConverter as ChemStation `.D` directories, each holding the
254 nm trace and ChemStation's peak report:

```{r read}
seq_dir <- system.file("extdata", "benzoxazinoid_standards",
                       package = "chromConverter")
chroms <- chromConverter::read_chroms(seq_dir, format_in = "chemstation_ch",
                                      pattern = "dad1A",
                                      parser = "chromconverter",
                                      progress_bar = FALSE)
names(chroms)
```

Shorter names make the tables easier to read, and moving the blank to the
end puts the runs in order of concentration. The standards were prepared by
serial dilution, so each is half the concentration of the one before; the
names round the last three, so `ppm` holds the exact values:

```{r ppm}
short_name <- function(x){
  x <- sub("BENZOS_(.*)PPM", "\\1 ppm", sub(",", ".", x))
  replace(x, x == "MEOH", "blank")
}
names(chroms) <- short_name(names(chroms))
ppm <- setNames(1000 / 2^(0:8), names(chroms)[-1])
chroms <- chroms[c(names(ppm), "blank")]
names(chroms)
```

The runs differ in length by a point, so `preprocess()` puts them on a
common time axis and removes the baseline. There is only one wavelength, so
`interpolate_cols = FALSE` leaves the spectral axis alone:

```{r preprocess}
chroms_pr <- preprocess(chroms, dim1 = seq(0, 59.9, by = 1/150),
                        interpolate_cols = FALSE, show_progress = FALSE)
```

## Retention time drift

With each run scaled to the height of its DIMBOA peak, the peak's movement
over the sequence is easy to see:

```{r fig-drift}
#| fig-cap: "DIMBOA in each standard before alignment, scaled to the same height. The grey band is the window `get_peaks()` searches by default: 0.1 minutes either side of DIMBOA's retention time in the 250 ppm run."
#| fig-alt: "The DIMBOA peak in each of the nine standards, scaled to the same height, coloured by concentration from 1000 to 4 ppm, with a grey band from 18.97 to 19.17 minutes. The peak sits at 19.1 minutes at 250 ppm, between 19.2 and 19.5 minutes in the other concentrated standards, and between 19.7 and 19.8 minutes in the four most dilute."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot the DIMBOA peak in each standard"
cols <- hcl.colors(length(ppm), "viridis")
plot_dimboa <- function(chroms, ...){
  times <- as.numeric(rownames(chroms[[1]]))
  near_dimboa <- times > 18.5 & times < 20.5
  dimboa <- sapply(chroms[names(ppm)], function(x){
    trace <- x[near_dimboa, 1]
    trace / max(trace)
  })
  matplot(times[near_dimboa], dimboa, type = "l", lty = 1, col = cols,
          xlab = "Retention time (min)", ylab = "Scaled absorbance", ...)
  rect(19.07 - 0.1, par("usr")[3], 19.07 + 0.1, par("usr")[4],
       col = adjustcolor("grey", 0.3), border = NA)
}
plot_dimboa(chroms_pr)
legend("topright", paste(signif(ppm, 3), "ppm"), col = cols, lty = 1,
       bty = "n")
```

DIMBOA elutes 0.7 minutes later in the dilute standards than in the 250 ppm
run, about twice its peak width, so a narrow window around its 250 ppm
retention time would miss it. The targets are at least 1.8 minutes apart, so
wide windows would also work here. In a crowded chromatogram, a wide window
would catch neighboring peaks, so aligning the runs keeps the windows narrow.

## Aligning the standards

The targets are listed at their retention times in the 250 ppm run:

```{r targets}
targets <- data.frame(name = c("DIBOA", "DIMBOA", "BOA", "MBOA"),
                      rt = c(12.54, 19.07, 20.98, 28.23))
```

The `correct_rt()` function works out how far to shift each part of a run to
line it up with the reference. This mapping is called a warp.
`get_peaks(mod_list = ...)` uses the warps to find each target in each run.
We can specify `time_unit = "s"` to report areas in mAU s, the unit 
ChemStation uses.

```{r tbl-unscaled}
#| tbl-cap: "Peak areas (mAU s) with the unscaled warp. A zero means no peak was found near the target."
# The drift nears the default max_shift of 1 minute. VPdtw's warnings about
# large shifts come only from stretches away from the targets.
warp_default <- suppressWarnings(
  correct_rt(chroms_pr, alg = "vpdtw", reference = "250 ppm",
             max_shift = 2, what = "models", show_progress = FALSE))
pks_default <- get_peaks(chroms_pr, targets = targets,
                         mod_list = warp_default, time_unit = "s",
                         show_progress = FALSE)
knitr::kable(get_peaktable(pks_default)$tab, digits = 0)
```

Targets go missing below 62.5 ppm, and none is found at 4 ppm. VPdtw matches
intensities, and the 4 ppm standard is 64 times more dilute than the
reference, so its peaks barely register.

`scale = TRUE` divides each run by its maximum before fitting the warp, so
the runs are compared by the shape of their signal:

```{r tbl-scaled}
#| tbl-cap: "Peak areas (mAU s) with `scale = TRUE`."
warp <- suppressWarnings(
  correct_rt(chroms_pr, alg = "vpdtw", reference = "250 ppm",
             scale = TRUE, max_shift = 2, what = "models",
             show_progress = FALSE))
pks <- get_peaks(chroms_pr, targets = targets, mod_list = warp,
                 time_unit = "s", show_progress = FALSE)
pk_tab <- get_peaktable(pks)
knitr::kable(pk_tab$tab, digits = 0)
```

Every target is now found in every standard. The blank has no targets, so
`get_peaks()` fitted the tallest bit of noise in each window.

Passing the warps back to `correct_rt()` through `models` returns the warped
chromatograms. Without scaling, DIMBOA lands outside the grey band at 31.25
and 4 ppm; with scaling, every standard lines up with the reference:

```{r fig-alignment}
#| fig-cap: "DIMBOA after each warp, scaled as in @fig-drift. A target is found only if its peak falls inside the grey band."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-alt: "Two panels showing the DIMBOA peak in each standard after alignment, scaled to the same height and coloured by concentration. Left, aligned without scaling: the peaks are spread between about 19.0 and 19.3 minutes, the 31.25 and 4 ppm peaks fall outside the grey band from 18.97 to 19.17 minutes, and several peaks are distorted. Right, aligned with scale = TRUE: all nine peaks lie inside the band, close to 19.1 minutes, and the two most dilute are broader and flat-topped."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot DIMBOA after each alignment"
warped_default <- correct_rt(chroms_pr, models = warp_default, alg = "vpdtw",
                             show_progress = FALSE)
warped <- correct_rt(chroms_pr, models = warp, alg = "vpdtw",
                     show_progress = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_dimboa(warped_default, main = "Without scaling")
plot_dimboa(warped, main = "scale = TRUE")
legend("topright", paste(signif(ppm, 3), "ppm"), col = cols, lty = 1,
       bty = "n")
```

## Peak integration

The warp only tells `get_peaks()` where to look; the peaks are fitted on the
unaligned chromatograms. Warping stretches and compresses peaks, as in the
flat tops of the two most dilute standards in @fig-alignment, so integrating the warped
chromatograms gives different areas:

```{r tbl-distortion}
#| tbl-cap: "Areas from the warped chromatograms, relative to areas from the unaligned ones."
pks_warped <- get_peaks(warped, targets = targets, time_unit = "s",
                        show_progress = FALSE)
distortion <- get_peaktable(pks_warped)$tab[names(ppm), ] /
  pk_tab$tab[names(ppm), ]
knitr::kable(distortion, digits = 2)
```

The areas from the warped chromatograms are off by up to
`r round(100 * max(abs(distortion - 1)))`%, most of all in the two most dilute
standards. Integrate the unaligned chromatograms, and use the warp only to
find the peaks.

## Fitting the calibration curves

Each compound's areas span more than two orders of magnitude, so an
unweighted fit would be dominated by the top standards. Weighting each
standard by `1 / ppm^2` gives every standard equal weight in relative terms.
To check the curves, convert each area back to a concentration and compare it
with the nominal one:

```{r tbl-errors}
#| tbl-cap: "Back-calculated error (%) against the nominal concentration."
fit_curve <- function(area, ppm) lm(area ~ ppm, weights = 1 / ppm^2)
quantify <- function(curve, area) (area - coef(curve)[[1]]) / coef(curve)[[2]]
areas <- pk_tab$tab[names(ppm), ]
curves <- lapply(areas, fit_curve, ppm = ppm)
errors <- 100 * (mapply(quantify, curves, areas) - ppm) / ppm
rownames(errors) <- names(ppm)
knitr::kable(errors, digits = 1)
```

Most standards back-calculate to within 10% of the nominal concentration. Above
about 30 ppm, each run's error is shared by all four compounds: every compound 
reads low at 1000 ppm and high at 62.5 ppm. Integration errors would differ
from one peak to the next, so an error all four compounds share points to the
run itself: that standard was more or less concentrated than its label says,
or more or less of it was injected.
Detector saturation can't explain the low readings at 1000 ppm, because BOA
never exceeds 300 mAU and reads as low as the others.

```{r fig-errors}
#| fig-cap: "Back-calculated errors from @tbl-errors."
#| fig-alt: "Percentage error of each back-calculated concentration against nominal concentration, one line per benzoxazinoid. Above about 30 ppm the four lines rise and fall together, reading high at 62.5 ppm and low at 500 and 1000 ppm. Below 30 ppm they separate."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot the errors"
matplot(ppm, errors, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 20, lty = 1, col = 1:4,
        xlab = "Concentration (ppm)", ylab = "Back-calculated error (%)")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey")
legend("topright", colnames(errors), col = 1:4, pch = 20, lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

Below about 30 ppm the compounds part ways. The smallest peaks are only a few
mAU tall, so a few mAU s of baseline error is a large fraction of their area.

On logarithmic axes, the dilute standards stay visible next to the
concentrated ones:

```{r fig-calibration}
#| fig-cap: "Calibration curves, fitted with weights of `1 / ppm^2`."
#| fig-alt: "Peak area against concentration for the four benzoxazinoids on logarithmic axes, from 4 to 1000 ppm, with a fitted calibration line through each compound's nine standards."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot the calibration curves"
grid <- exp(seq(log(min(ppm)), log(max(ppm)), length.out = 50))
fitted <- sapply(curves, predict, newdata = data.frame(ppm = grid))
matplot(ppm, areas, log = "xy", pch = 20, col = 1:4,
        xlab = "Concentration (ppm)", ylab = "Peak area (mAU s)")
matlines(grid, fitted, lty = 1, col = 1:4)
legend("topleft", colnames(areas), col = 1:4, pch = 20, bty = "n")
```

## Quantifying an "unknown"

`quantify()` solves a curve for the concentration that gives a sample's area.
This dataset holds no unknowns, so the 31.25 ppm standard stands in for one:
fit the curves to the other eight standards, then quantify it and the blank:

```{r tbl-quantify}
#| tbl-cap: "Concentrations (ppm) from curves fitted without the 31.25 ppm standard."
unknown <- "31.25 ppm"
standards <- setdiff(names(ppm), unknown)
curves_8 <- lapply(areas[standards, ], fit_curve, ppm = ppm[standards])
samples <- pk_tab$tab[c(unknown, "blank"), ]
concentration <- mapply(quantify, curves_8, samples)
rownames(concentration) <- rownames(samples)
knitr::kable(concentration, digits = 1)
```

All four compounds in the `r ppm[[unknown]]` ppm standard read
`r paste(round(range(100 * (concentration[unknown, ] / ppm[[unknown]] - 1))), collapse = " to ")`%
high. As in the calibration fit, an error shared by every compound points to
the run (a dilution step, evaporation from the vial, or the injection volume)
rather than the integration. The blank reads slightly below zero because the
curve is extrapolating below the lowest standard. Report such samples as below
`r round(min(ppm))` ppm, not as a number.

## Comparing integration results with ChemStation

ChemStation integrated the same runs when they were acquired, and its peak
reports ship with the data. Its retention times are not aligned, so each
target's window has to cover the drift, from just before its 250 ppm
retention time to 0.8 minutes after. The largest peak in the window is the
target:

```{r chemstation}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Match ChemStation's peaks to the targets"
peak_list <- chromConverter::read_peaklist(seq_dir, format_in = "chemstation",
                                           progress_bar = FALSE)
reports <- do.call(rbind, lapply(peak_list, `[[`, "254"))
reports$sample <- short_name(reports$sample)
cs <- lapply(targets$rt, function(target_rt){
  in_window <- subset(reports, rt > target_rt - 0.1 & rt < target_rt + 0.8)
  in_window <- in_window[order(in_window$area, decreasing = TRUE), ]
  in_window[match(names(ppm), in_window$sample), ]
})
cs_areas <- sapply(cs, `[[`, "area")
cs_heights <- sapply(cs, `[[`, "height")
dimnames(cs_areas) <- dimnames(cs_heights) <- list(names(ppm), targets$name)
```

The two programs draw the baseline differently: chromatographR fits it to
the whole run, while ChemStation draws a line under each peak (see the
[FAQ](FAQ.html)). `get_peaks(baseline = "flat")` also fits a constant offset
under each peak:

```{r flat-baseline}
pks_flat <- get_peaks(chroms_pr, targets = targets, mod_list = warp,
                      baseline = "flat", time_unit = "s",
                      show_progress = FALSE)
areas_flat <- get_peaktable(pks_flat)$tab[names(ppm), ]
```

Two MBOA peaks show the difference: at 8 ppm the two programs differ most,
and at 31.25 ppm only the flat baseline differs from ChemStation:

```{r fig-chemstation}
#| fig-cap: "(a) chromatographR's areas relative to ChemStation's, without a local baseline (filled) and with a flat one (open). Arrows mark the MBOA peaks in b to e. (b to e) MBOA at 8 and 31.25 ppm without a local baseline (b, d) and with a flat one (c, e); the shaded area is the fitted peak."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-alt: "Five panels. Panel a: ratio of chromatographR's peak area to ChemStation's against ChemStation's peak height, one colour per benzoxazinoid, filled for no local baseline and open for a flat local baseline. Above about 5 mAU the two sets of points coincide, between 0.95 and 1.03. Below 5 mAU the filled points rise to 1.24, while the open points lie between 0.88 and 1.05. Vertical arrows run from the filled to the open point for each MBOA peak shown in panels panels b-e. Panels b-e: the 8 ppm MBOA peak, about 1.1 mAU tall, and the 31.25 ppm MBOA peak, about 3.7 mAU tall, with the fitted peak shaded and a dotted line at zero absorbance. Without a local baseline (b, d) the shaded peak reaches down to zero, below the trace on either side. With a flat local baseline (c, e) the shaded peak sits on the level of the trace on either side."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot the comparison"
examples <- data.frame(sample = c("8 ppm", "31.25 ppm"),
                       rt = c(28.92, 28.84), ymax = c(1.2, 4))
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 4, 1, 3, 5), 2, byrow = TRUE), widths = c(1.6, 1, 1))
matplot(cs_heights, areas / cs_areas, log = "x", pch = 16, col = 1:4,
        ylim = range(areas / cs_areas, areas_flat / cs_areas),
        xlab = "Peak height in ChemStation (mAU)",
        ylab = "Area ratio (chromatographR / ChemStation)")
matpoints(cs_heights, areas_flat / cs_areas, pch = 1, col = 1:4)
abline(h = 1, col = "grey")
legend("topright", c(colnames(areas), 'baseline = "none"', 'baseline = "flat"'),
       pch = c(rep(15, 4), 16, 1), col = c(1:4, 1, 1), bty = "n", ncol = 2)
for (i in 1:2){
  s <- examples$sample[i]
  example_ratio <- c(areas[s, "MBOA"], areas_flat[s, "MBOA"]) /
    cs_areas[s, "MBOA"]
  arrows(cs_heights[s, "MBOA"], example_ratio[1] - 0.01,
         y1 = example_ratio[2] + 0.01, length = 0.08, col = "grey20")
  text(cs_heights[s, "MBOA"], example_ratio, letters[2 * i + 0:1],
       pos = 4, font = 2)
}
mtext("a", side = 3, adj = 0, line = 0.5, font = 2)
for (i in 1:2){
  for (j in 1:2){
    plot(list(pks, pks_flat)[[j]], idx = examples$sample[i],
         targets = examples$rt[i], ylim = c(0, examples$ymax[i]),
         main = sprintf('%s, baseline = "%s"', examples$sample[i],
                        c("none", "flat")[j]),
         cex.main = 1, xlab = "Retention time (min)",
         ylab = "Absorbance (mAU)")
    abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
    mtext(letters[2 * i + j - 1], side = 3, adj = 0, line = 0.5, font = 2)
  }
}
```

Above about 5 mAU, both sets of areas are within about 5% of ChemStation's,
and most are a few percent smaller. Below 5 mAU they diverge. Without a local
baseline, areas are up to a quarter larger: the whole-run baseline leaves a
little signal under the smallest peaks, and the fit includes it (b, d). The
flat baseline sits on the trace on either side (c, e) and ranges from 12%
below ChemStation to 5% above, yet ChemStation agrees with it at 8 ppm and
with no local baseline at 31.25 ppm. Without peaks of known area, this
comparison can't say which integration is right, only that below about 5 mAU
the choice of baseline alone moves the area by up to
`r round(100 * max(abs(1 - areas_flat / areas)))`%.

The two most dilute MBOA standards are the hardest to integrate: their peaks
are about 1 mAU tall, and the flat baseline shrinks their areas by about a
fifth. They still back-calculate to within
`r ceiling(max(abs(errors[c("8 ppm", "4 ppm"), "MBOA"])))`% of
nominal, about as close as the other standards, so they can stay in the
curve, but concentrations this low are less certain than the fit suggests.

## See also

- The [`targeted_analysis`](../reference/targeted_analysis.html) help page
  describes the other route to a table of targets, which this article doesn't
  use: matching peaks to a reference sample by spectrum with `match_peaks()`,
  for targets that retention time alone can't pick out but whose spectra are
  distinct from their neighbors'.
- [chromConverter's vignette](https://ethanbass.github.io/chromConverter/articles/chromConverter.html)
  works through the same files: reading the sequence, its metadata and the
  ChemStation reports.
